summary: Virtual Network Computing software provides remote desktop functionality. This informational RFC describes a URI scheme that lets other applications launch VNC clients, with parameters useful for securely connecting to remote hosts.

plainLanguage.summary: A web-style link that, when clicked, opens a remote-desktop program and connects it to the right computer.

subtitle: A web-style link that launches VNC remote-desktop clients with connection details and security options.

tldr.problem: VNC (Virtual Network Computing) clients provide remote desktop access, but applications wanting to launch VNC clients had no standard way to specify connection parameters, making integration difficult.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7869 defines a vnc:// URI scheme with a host, port, and optional parameters for authentication, security type, connection channels (SSH or TLS tunneling), and visual settings. Applications can click or invoke a VNC URI, and the client handles the rest.
tldr.outcome: Browsers, web applications, and other programs can now launch VNC clients without being tied to a specific client implementation, using secure tunneling options to protect credentials and data in transit.

facts.label: Channel types
facts.value: Standard TCP (1), Secure Tunnel (23), Integrated SSH (24)

today: RFC 7869 is an Informational RFC that specifies the VNC URI scheme. It has not been obsoleted and remains the standard for launching VNC clients with a URI.

sections.title: Remote Desktop and URI Integration
sections.content:
Virtual Network Computing (VNC) software provides remote desktop functionality, allowing a user to see and control a computer from another machine. VNC is based on the Remote Framebuffer (RFB) Protocol, which transmits screen images and mouse and keyboard input. However, VNC clients lacked a standard way to be launched from other applications with connection parameters.

RFC 7869 solves this by defining a vnc:// URI scheme. Like an http:// link that opens a browser, a vnc:// link can launch a VNC client with all the information needed to connect, from a web page, email, or other application. This enables seamless integration without tying users to one particular VNC client.
sections.plainLanguage: Just as clicking a web link opens your browser, clicking a VNC link opens your remote-control program and connects it to the right computer.

sections.title: The VNC URI Structure
sections.content:
A VNC URI begins with vnc:// followed by a host address (hostname or IP) and an optional port (default 5900). After that, optional parameters are specified using standard URL query strings with ?param=value¶m=value syntax. For example:

vnc://10.0.0.1:5901?VncPassword=secret&SecurityType=2&ViewOnly=false

The main parameters include: ConnectionName (a profile name to save), VncUsername and VncPassword (for VNC authentication), SecurityType (which RFB security mechanism to use, from the IANA registry), ColorLevel (display color depth), ViewOnly (if true, prevent keyboard and mouse input), and SaveConnection (whether to save the connection profile for later use).
sections.plainLanguage: A VNC URI tells your remote-control program three things: where to find the computer, how to log in, and what settings to use.

sections.title: Secure Tunneling: SSH and TLS
sections.content:
VNC traffic can be insecure if sent directly. To protect credentials and data, RFC 7869 defines two secure connection channel types: SSH tunneling and TLS tunneling. With Integrated SSH (ChannelType=24), the client first establishes an SSH connection to a server, authenticates with an SSH username and password, and then opens a tunnel through SSH to the VNC server. This provides encryption, data integrity, and verification of the SSH server's public key or certificate via an IdHash parameter. With Secure Tunnel (ChannelType=23), the client establishes a TLS connection with certificate authentication, and then connects to VNC through that secure tunnel.

Both methods support the IdHashAlgorithm parameter to specify which hash algorithm (MD5, SHA1, or SHA256) is used to compute and verify the server's certificate or key hash.
sections.plainLanguage: Secure tunneling means your VNC connection goes through an encrypted wrapper (like SSH) so nobody listening on the network can see your password or what you are doing.

sections.title: SSH and Advanced Parameters
sections.content:
When using SSH tunneling, additional parameters control the SSH connection: SshHost (defaults to the host if not specified), SshPort (default 22), SshUsername, and SshPassword. VNC clients can also match an incoming URI to a stored connection profile in the client's local database using the ConnectionName parameter. If a profile exists with that name, the client applies any settings from the profile that are not already specified in the URI, allowing users to save common configurations and reuse them.

Parameter names are case-insensitive for flexibility, but values are case-sensitive. Clients MAY support client-specific parameters with a distinguishing prefix (like com.dell.vncclient.ScreenMode) for advanced features.
sections.plainLanguage: You can save connection settings to reuse them later, and clients can understand both standard parameters and their own special tricks.

sections.title: Security Risks and Best Practices
sections.content:
VNC URIs can contain sensitive information like passwords, usernames, and host addresses. The RFC warns that credentials and host information could be exposed through process listings, logs, or browser caches if not handled carefully. Users should avoid including credentials in URIs passed through untrusted channels or applications that are known to log or cache data insecurely.

Since the RFB protocol itself may not encrypt data, always use SSH or TLS tunneling for security. Strong passwords or key-based authentication are essential. VNC clients should verify remote host identity using certificate hashes to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks. Applications launching VNC clients should only do so from trusted sources, and users should verify application integrity when installing them.
sections.plainLanguage: Never put a password in a VNC link that could be seen by others. Always use encryption for the tunnel. Check that you are connecting to the real computer you expect, not a fake one.

sections.title: IANA Registration and Registries
sections.content: The vnc scheme is registered as a permanent Uniform Resource Identifier scheme with IANA. RFC 7869 also establishes several IANA registries to support the scheme: the VNC URI Connection Channel Types registry (for channel types like Standard TCP, Secure Tunnel, and Integrated SSH), the VNC URI ID Hash Algorithms registry (for MD5, SHA1, and SHA256), and the VNC URI Parameters registry (for all standard parameters). These registries allow vendors to add new channel types, hash algorithms, and parameters following a First Come First Served process, enabling the scheme to evolve without revising the RFC itself.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps official lists of the channel types and parameters that VNC URIs support, so new ones can be added without changing the standard.
